content: A mixture in chemistry is a substance formed by combining two or more different materials without any chemical reaction taking place. In a mixture, the individual components do not chemically bond with each other. These mixtures can typically be separated back into their original components. Examples of mixtures include fruit salad, ocean water, and soil. Some heterogeneous mixtures include salt water, iron filings, sulfur, and salt mixed with sand. Mixtures result from the mechanical blending or mixing of chemical substances, such as elements and compounds, without any chemical bonding or chemical changes. Each component in a mixture retains its own chemical properties and composition. Although there are no chemical changes in a mixture, its physical properties, such as melting point, may differ from those of its individual components. Mixtures can generally be separated using mechanical methods. They are classified as either homogeneous or heterogeneous. Homogeneous Mixtures Homogeneous mixtures are those with uniform and consistent properties throughout. The particles in these mixtures are evenly distributed, meaning that any portion of the mixture has the same composition and properties as any other portion. Examples of homogeneous mixtures include solutions and some alloys (though not all alloys are homogeneous). A homogeneous mixture consists of only one phase. Examples include gasoline and margarine. Solutions A solution is a type of homogeneous mixture in which one or more substances (called solutes) are dissolved in another substance (called the solvent). In a solution, the particles are extremely small, typically less than 1 nanometer (nm) in size, and can include atoms, small molecules, or small ions. A common example of a solution is a solid dissolving into a liquid, such as salt or sugar dissolving in water, or gold dissolving in mercury. Liquids can also dissolve into one another, and in some cases, liquids can dissolve into gases, such as water vapor mixing with the atmosphere. A familiar example of a solution is a carbonated beverage, where carbon dioxide is dissolved in the liquid through carbonation. Solutions exhibit properties known as colligative properties, which change depending on the concentration of the solute. Solubility is a key property of compounds in solutions. Colloidal Dispersions Colloids are another type of homogeneous mixture, but they differ from solutions in that the particles of one or more components are larger, typically ranging from 1 to 1000 nanometers (nm) in size. These particles are larger than those in a solution but smaller than those in a suspension. A colloid, or colloidal dispersion, consists of components that may exist in one or two phases. Colloids exhibit the Tyndall effect, which occurs when light passes through the mixture and is scattered by the particles. Unlike suspensions, colloids do not settle over time. Examples of colloidal dispersions include jelly, milk, blood, paint, fog, and glue. Heterogeneous Mixtures Heterogeneous mixtures are those with an inconsistent and non-uniform composition. The individual components of a heterogeneous mixture can be mechanically separated from one another. Examples of heterogeneous mixtures include salad, trail mix, and granite. Suspensions A suspension is a type of heterogeneous mixture in which the particles of at least one component are larger than 1 micrometer (1000 nanometers) in at least one dimension. These particles are larger than those found in colloids. Unlike colloids, the particles in a suspension will eventually settle if left undisturbed. An example of a suspension is sand mixed with water. Particles in suspensions are large enough to scatter light, a phenomenon known as the Tyndall effect.
